title: A Theoretical Digital Twin Framework for Multi-Stage Point-of-Use Water Purification Systems: Sensor Fusion and Stochastic Remaining Useful Life Prediction
abstract: Decentralized Point-of-Use (POU) water purification systems face extreme influent variability, yet current maintenance relies on reactive schedules, risking membrane failure. This study proposes a theoretical Digital Twin framework to overcome these vulnerabilities. We developed a 15-sensor topology across seven analytical nodes, using mass-balance equations to bypass physical sensors on the reverse osmosis (RO) reject stream. Component-specific degradation models—Hermia’s physical clogging, Yoon–Nelson adsorptive exhaustion, and solution–diffusion—were integrated into a Bayesian Particle Filter coupled with a Gamma process. This algorithm dynamically processes simulated noisy IoT sensor data to estimate the system’s Remaining Useful Life (RUL) and State of Health (SoH). Computational simulations under extreme operational scenarios demonstrated the framework’s ability to decouple physical fouling from chemical exhaustion. To address the lack of a physical prototype, internal consistency and algorithmic robustness were verified through Monte Carlos simulations under varied noise profiles, yielding high empirical interval coverage. The stochastic model adaptively updated RUL predictions, accurately tracking the sigmoidal chlorine breakthrough curve to protect the RO membrane. This framework provides a scalable, mathematical architecture for transitioning to Condition-Based Maintenance, establishing a foundation for future physical validation and deployment.
title_zh: A Theoretical Digital Twin Framework for Multi-Stage Point-of-Use Water Purification Systems: Sensor Fusion and Stochastic Remaining Useful Life Prediction

title: An Operational Digital Twin for Electric Bus Depot Charging Infrastructure: Validation and Scenario Analysis at a Sub-Saharan African Fleet
abstract: Charging infrastructure for battery electric bus (BEB) fleets must be sized against the timing of demand, not only its magnitude: an accurate per-trip energy estimate cannot on its own establish whether a depot’s chargers, contracted grid connection, and dispatch schedule can recover the fleet’s energy deficit without breaching demand-based tariff thresholds. This is especially consequential in resource-constrained settings, where notified-maximum-demand penalties and steep time-of-use differentials turn a mistimed charging load into a direct commercial liability rather than an operational inconvenience. Yet pre-investment planning tools typically treat vehicle energy consumption, dispatch scheduling, and charging infrastructure as separate problems, so a validated demand estimate rarely translates into a validated depot load profile. This paper presents an operational digital twin that converts the per-trip arrival state-of-charge predicted by a companion rolling stock twin into a depot-level charging load profile for the Golden Arrow Bus Services (GABS) electric fleet at the Arrowgate depot in Cape Town, South Africa. The twin reconstructs each bus’s daily duty chain from scheduling data to determine its available charging window, then simulates session initiation, power draw, and duration against these windows using charging behaviour parametrised from depot Open Charge Point Protocol (OCPP) records, including the smart charging constraints already enforced at the depot. Each bus’s state of charge is carried from one depot visit to the next, so an undercharged departure reappears as a lower arrival rather than disappearing from the model. The simulated load profile is validated against 968 OCPP session records from two periods with different depot hardware, achieving energy-per-session agreement of 4.5 to 7.3% and load-shape correlation of 0.95 to 0.99; on a held-out night not used for calibration, with every recorded session as input, the twin reproduces the depot’s measured overnight peak to within 3.3%, and on a July day with no site pool, with nothing calibrated, its mean overnight load to within 0.8%. The simulated load profile is evaluated against the depot’s contracted notified maximum demand of 3000 kVA. Scenario analysis quantifies how the charging schedule, charger rate, and site pool limit shift the load profile relative to this threshold and to time-of-use cost exposure, showing that scheduling charging into off-peak windows without a site-wide limit can raise peak demand above uncontrolled charging and beyond the contracted threshold (3167 against 1832 kW), that a site pool limit controls peak demand and monthly cost together, and that a 30 kW per-charger cap leaves buses unable to complete up to 15% of their trips; grown to 80 buses, the fleet would exceed the depot’s 2025 connector count before its pool limit, which the twin shows as overnight queueing and stranded trips. By coupling a validated, condition-aware demand layer to depot dispatch and charging logic, this work supports capital-efficient charging-infrastructure decisions for transit operators facing demand-based tariffs and constrained grid capacity, as at Arrowgate, where undersized infrastructure risks service disruption and oversized infrastructure diverts capital from wider electrification.
title_zh: An Operational Digital Twin for Electric Bus Depot Charging Infrastructure: Validation and Scenario Analysis at a Sub-Saharan African Fleet

title: Recent Advances in Sensing Materials for Monitoring Thermal Runaway in Lithium-Ion Batteries
abstract: Lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) play a critical role in modern energy technologies, powering portable electronics, electric vehicles, and renewable energy storage systems due to their high energy density, long cycle life, and lightweight properties. However, their high energy storage capacity presents intrinsic safety challenges posed by thermal runaway, a potentially catastrophic failure mode. Recent advances in safety monitoring leverage detectable thermal runaway precursors, including temperature fluctuations, pressure variations, and gas evolution. Although significant efforts have focused on developing smart materials for early-stage thermal runaway detection, limited reviews have systematically addressed these material innovations. This review seeks to fill this gap by providing a concise overview of the mechanisms underlying thermal runaway in LIBs and the corresponding smart monitoring strategies. It also examines recent progress in smart materials tailored for temperature, pressure, and gas sensing applications. The primary objective of this survey is to offer valuable insights and guidance for enhancing thermal runaway safety management in battery systems.
title_zh: Recent Advances in Sensing Materials for Monitoring Thermal Runaway in Lithium-Ion Batteries
